articles.title: This week in Tom's Hardware Premium: November 14, 2026 — Mac Studio versus DGX Spark, AMD's MEXT cuts DRAM requirements in half, and the Huang saga reaches critical mass
articles.content: Seismic appears to set the tone for this week's events in the hardware industry, and we've covered the biggest beats, including deeper dives on hardware and AI topics over on Tom's Hardware Premium . Stories this week are colored by the fact that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has stepped away from his post as CEO. The ramifications are wide and far-reaching, as the company transformed from a gaming GPU manufacturer to an AI business over the past five years. First up, it's not only hyperscalers and neoclouds that have their eyes on AI. An increasingly popular segment among enthusiasts is PCs dedicated to running local AI models. With so many choices on the market currently, from the recently released RTX Spark to AMD's Strix Halo platform, we take a look at two unlikely contenders that are now going head-to-head: Nvidia's DGX Spark and Apple's Mac Studio. We ran a suite of real-world and synthetic benchmarks across both devices and tested large models on both machines. With prices at eye-watering levels, it's more crucial than ever that you make the correct choice for your intended workloads. Going deep on local AI performance benchmarking with Apple’s Mac Studio with M5 Ultra taking on Nvidia DGX Spark — inference engine recipes mandatory for bigger models as MLX stack matures DRAM capacity constraints have been an industry-wide sticking point as the AI buildout accelerates demand for dies. With costs spiraling across both client and enterprise hardware, AMD has shared further detail about MEXT, a predictive memory engine which aims to offer 99% of a server's performance while running on half the DRAM. Powered by a transformer model and clever use of flash storage, AMD is already running 145 servers with the system in place, with a view to expand that figure to 2,000 next year. AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT — tech powers over 100 servers already running, with plans to expand to 2,000 servers in 2027 Next, we sat down with Cognichip's Chief Product Officer in an extensive interview to explore how the company is rolling out AI-powered chip design tools. Back in September, the company revealed a suite of proprietary AI models, named Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), which are specifically developed for semiconductor engineering. While the tools have yet to be used in a shipping product, it could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks. Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Jensen Huang scandal deepens, as the now-former Nvidia CEO has become embroiled in a series of alleged extramarital affairs and has since resigned from Nvidia. While much of the past week's stories have centered on his relationship with alleged Chinese Spy Alice Huang, we explored the former CEO's unlikely relationship with Kang Wei, Ms. Huang's husband, who recently landed in hot water with China's Securities Regulatory Commission. How Shanghai fund manager Kang Wei introduced his wife Alice Huang to Jensen and built a $7.5 billion Nvidia AI GPU smuggling operation — Mistress's husband joked she was the Nvidia CEO's 'personal assistant' Nvidia-based compute remains difficult to find in China, especially as AI labs line up to order racks and newer cards like the RTX 5500 Pro, with over 6 million units reportedly ordered for the export-compliant GB202-based AI accelerator. But the Chinese AI labs that are chasing after Nvidia's tech may still have to pay a premium and ensure that they're running enough homegrown silicon to not fall afoul of Beijing's rules. We explore how some companies have now moved to renting compute in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore in an attempt to get around export controls. Nvidia cracks down on…

articles.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
articles.content: AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth , try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training. “Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.” Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess. This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer. The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools. Web results Internal data Freshness Often hours or days old Can be months out of date without anyone noticing Quality Uneven: official docs next to forum threads Curated, but written for a past state of the product Structure Mostly unstructured text Mix of text, metadata and structured records Authority Has to be inferred from the source Known, but rarely stored as a field Access control Public Per customer, region, contract or role The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it? Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available. Why concatenating results breaks in production The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways: Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers. A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does. “A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of…

articles.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
articles.content: How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast. DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity. In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS . The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda , lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation. “These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack . Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.” DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work. “The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.” Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing. Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer. DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum. “One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.” “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.” During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition . “With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and…

articles.title: U.S. Treasury Secretary questions whether Nvidia knowingly sold AI GPUs to shell companies, says company itself is responsible
articles.content: Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary, admitted that the U.S. export controls cannot prevent all the restricted hardware from reaching China or other adversaries, which is why the country allegedly obtained millions of restricted AI GPUs from Nvidia . At the same time, he questioned the efficiency of Nvidia's internal controls. called for accountability at Nvidia, criticized the company's general counsel, but stressed that it was unclear whether Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang knew about the potentially illicit practices. Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs (Image credit: Noctua) Desktop GPU Roadmap Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026? Rubin in-depth The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down," in an interview with CNBC (via @siliconmemes ). "One thing here is that the story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles. The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? And I think it is important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent admitted that despite strict U.S. export controls that prohibit sales of advanced AI GPUs to China, considerable quantities of restricted hardware may still make their way to the country. However, the Treasury Secretary does not believe that the U.S. needs to introduce more stringent export restrictions or grant government agencies additional powers to prevent GPU smuggling. Instead, the authorities should properly enforce existing regulations, according to Bessent. Bessent also criticized Nvidia's general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly contacted the U.S. Department of Commerce to inquire whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. However, the Treasury Secretary declined to speculate about potential consequences for Nvidia if it turned out that some of its executives knew that their customers acted as intermediaries for Chinese entities. Meanwhile, Bessent expressed confidence that Nvidia's board of directors would conduct a thorough investigation into the matter. "But let us just say, if this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the company," Bessent said. "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this. The [general council] seems to have been very involved here, probably should have done more oversight rather than the haranguing [government officials at the U.S. DoC]." Bessent also revealed that the Departments of the Treasury, War, and State, as well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), had supported the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List for months. However, the authority to impose such export restrictions belongs to the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which reportedly stalled efforts to blacklist Megaspeed for months as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick feared that the move could worsen trade tensions with China.
articles.author: Anton Shilov

articles.content: PC Gamer reports: The Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, a "free national videogame development competition for students," has confirmed that the rise of generative AI means this year's event will be the last... Speculation as to the cause of the program's cancellation focused primarily on the presence of AI in entries: Another self-proclaimed judge said the problem wasn't merely the use of AI in itself but that "some students just completely generate their games with AI...." [T]he Australian Council for Educational Research has confirmed that the cancellation was in fact due to AI.... "making it harder to judge what students made themselves, and moving the program away from its original purpose." Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader neoRUR for sharing the news. articles.title: We tested the RAM-saving storage tech in Gears of War: E-Day
articles.content: Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies. However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage. We’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems. The Storage Tech Explained The Storage Tech Explained In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM. Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience. Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates. Is this storage tech also used on PC? Is this storage tech also used on PC? YouTuber Mostly Positive Review s shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game. Gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data.My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well.These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often. October 7, 2026 Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality. articles.title: The FAA’s IT troubles are far bigger then AI
articles.content: U.S. airlines are still reeling from a nationwide groundstop issued late Friday night that interrupted weekend travel and wreaked havoc on schedules. The culprit, the Federal Aviation Administration says, was simply outdated tech. The groundstop was followed by eager speculation on social media about what might have caused the issue. Some pointed a finger at a new AI system that the FAA integrated earlier this week; others blamed foreign adversaries. At the same time, a range of tech companies that contract with the FAA (like Microsoft ) were quick to distance themselves from the agency’s problems. Later Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters the outage occurred after an old Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) analog system, an arcane system of processing data signals over a network, became overloaded. This, in turn, impacted the telecommunications systems used by TRACONs, the air traffic control facilities that help direct flights at airports. Duffy noted that systems that had already been upgraded to new internet protocol-based systems did not experience the outage. “This is all the old legacy equipment,” he said Friday . “All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down.” Officials, at least for now, insist there’s no evidence anything nefarious happened. Instead, the Transportation Department is, once again, begging Congress for more money to overhaul FAA tech. Duffy urged Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system, arguing that the issue should transcend partisan politics. He noted that the FAA had received $15 billion for modernization efforts over the past 25 years, with little to show for it. “It’s not red, it’s not blue, it’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican, it’s American,” he told reporters. “Give us the money to fix it.” Indeed, the FAA’s tech problems are way bigger than AI. Instead, they have a lot more to do with the challenges of updating technology while it’s actively being used. Our pilots guidance system is ancient and isn’t designed to handle upgrades This isn’t the first time the FAA has experienced a major outage that’s brought flights across the country to a halt. Back in 2023, the U.S.’s Notice to Airmen system (NOTAM)—which alerts pilots to potential hazards in American airspace—came offline, after contractors accidentally deleted files that disrupted the program’s core technology. There’s been an ongoing effort to improve the NOTAM system, but it’s moving at a snail’s pace. The FAA has brought in private industry for help and engaged in an effort to modernize the system, but that process has only brought to light myriad other problems. For one, at least according to contract paperwork obtained last year , NOTAMs weren’t exclusively being stored in a virtual environment or in an entirely-digital format. Another aspiration the FAA was working on, at least at the time: making sure that upgrades to some systems didn’t disrupt, well, all of air traffic control. “Everyone will say, ‘well, there’s backups in place,’” Shawn Pruchnicki, a former pilot atOhio State’s Center for Aviation Studies, told FedScoop at the time. “But we’ve also seen time and time again where those things have been said and things have gone horribly wrong.” Poor AI rollout Like a lot of other federal agencies, the Federal Aviation Administration has been inching toward deploying artificial intelligence for a host of applications. Back in 2023, the Transportation Department, which the FAA sits under, even disclosed using ChatGPT for certain purposes (which the FAA, at the time, denied). Since then, though, the FAA begun to embrace AI: A use case inventory released by the government references several use cases, including AI-powered pilot voice transcription, systems for detecting drones, and meteorology. But the FAA hasn’t been the best at communicating how it plans to use AI safely to the public,…

articles.title: Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch.
articles.content: Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude , but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that the company supplying their models could eventually become their biggest competitor. A nervous warning to wrappers Gerald Zingraf , president and COO of GlacierGrid, raised the concern on LinkedIn following Anthropic’s Tuesday expansion of Claude’s enterprise lineup, comparing its strategy to Amazon’s private-label business. “Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” Zingraf writes, drawing on his experience selling products he designed through Amazon before watching the retailer introduce competing products. “Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” His concern is that Anthropic can see which third-party integrations customers use most frequently and potentially draw on that information when deciding which capabilities to build itself. “Anthropic has the same view,” he argues, although he offers no evidence that the company uses integration data to identify competitors or inform its product roadmap. For some developers, the risk is no longer hypothetical. When partners become rivals Scott Stevenson , CEO of legal AI startup Spellbook, described what happened when Anthropic moved into his company’s market in a November 2 interview with Forbes . Spellbook uses Claude models for everything from reviewing contracts and suggesting revisions to automating legal workflows. Stevenson recalls Anthropic employees assuring him the company had no plans to compete directly in legal software, before Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, which includes contract-review capabilities that overlap with Spellbook’s business. “Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” “Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” Stevenson said in the interview. “Ultimately this is inevitable.” Spellbook hasn’t abandoned Claude. Anthropic still features the startup as a customer , reporting roughly 530,000 monthly contract reviews performed by its Claude-powered agents, while Stevenson also appears in Anthropic’s October 28 announcement of legal artifacts . The relationship illustrates a difficult position for developers whose products depend on frontier models. Spellbook still benefits from Anthropic’s technology, even as Anthropic develops applications aimed at some of the same customers. Nothing in Stevenson’s account establishes that Anthropic used Spellbook’s proprietary information to develop its legal offering. When the platform ships your product Tech founder and Dalton Mills CEO Todd Saunders made a similar argument in a March 10 post on X , following Anthropic’s introduction of Claude Code Review . “Anthropic is the new Amazon,” “Anthropic is the new Amazon,” Saunders writes, warning developers building on Claude’s SDK that the company could observe application usage and eventually incorporate competing functionality into Claude. The company’s November 10 announcement introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, while previewing Claude Meetings. Expanded interactive connectors also let partners embed applications directly inside Claude, including software from Adobe and Atlassian. What the policies leave unsaid Anthropic has access to information about how customers interact with third-party apps and services, something the company acknowledges in its privacy policy , effective September 10, 2026. What isn’t clear is whether Anthropic looks at which integrations are most popular when deciding what to build next. The rules are different for business customers. Under Anthropic’s…

articles.title: FlexiSpot's E7 Pro standing desk has prices starting from just $399.99 in the Black Friday sale
articles.content: The FlexiSpot E7 Pro is one of our favorite standing desks, and its various configurations are now listed in Black Friday sales, which makes it an even more attractive option for anyone who wants a little more movement in their day-to-day. The E7 Pro combines a sturdy steel frame, dual monitors, and generous height adjustment with optional cable management to make it an exceptional choice. Today's best FlexiSpot E7 Pro Black Friday deal The FlexiSpot E7 Pro is currently listed at $399.99 on the manufacturer's website. That investment gets you the frame without cable management - if you want different kinds of tabletop, cable management options, or accessories, the prices change. However, everything is on offer for Black Friday, so you’ll be getting a decent discount no matter which product you buy. View Deal Why we recommend the FlexiSpot E7 Pro The E7 Pro is an electric standing desk that features dual motors, a height adjustment range of 25 to 50.6 inches, and a sturdy C-shaped steel frame. It also offers four programmable height presets, a cable tray, and a magnetic cable cover. We reviewed the E7 Pro, and it earned an Editor’s Choice award. Our reviewer was impressed with its robust construction, rock-solid stability, and its wide variety of attractive desktop finishes. When moving, its motors were quiet, and assembly took a reasonable thirty-five minutes. The controls are intuitive, so it’s easy to switch between sitting and standing positions. There are a couple of drawbacks. The desk commands a premium price, particularly with some desktop configurations, and its heavier construction can make moving it around difficult. Read our full FlexiSpot E7 Pro standing desk review Price context and historical value At $399.99 the E7 Pro is a very good deal for a premium standing desk - that's a substantial saving on the standard price of $499.99. Bear in mind that $399.99 is the Black Friday price for the frame only. If you want to add in cable management then the frame is $519.99. Adding the entry-level laminate tabletop to the E7 Pro frame costs an extra $90; adding it to the frame with cable management, too, costs an extra $320. The other tabletops are more expensive. You're paying more than you would for a basic electric standing desk, but the dual motors, excellent stability, cable management, and 15-year warranty help justify the investment. It’s pricey, sure, but it’s an excellent product that could easily last you decades. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the FlexiSpot E7 Pro if... you want a premium, sturdy standing desk with quiet dual motors, programmable height settings, and excellent cable management. It's a particularly good choice for a permanent home office. ❌ Skip the FlexiSpot E7 Pro if... you're on a tight budget or simply need a basic height-adjustable desk. Cheaper alternatives are available, and you may not need all its premium features.

articles.title: Malaysia plans new law using data center power consumption to catch AI GPU smugglers
articles.content: Malaysia plans to introduce a new law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail . The authorities also plan to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws. Malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically. The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage. Meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia. While data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads. Furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors. Johari said that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the new legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections. Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

articles.title: Canva just launched its own AI image generator, so I tested it vs ChatGPT
articles.content: Online design tool Canva has just launched Canva Craft , its first AI image generation model that lets you make all sorts of visual content to add to the things you create. So think social media and marketing materials, lifestyle photography, digital art, characters, nature imagery and more. If you already rely on ChatGPT or another AI tool to create visuals for you but you also regularly use Canva, it could be a good way to combine image generation and design in one. And although it may not be as powerful as ChatGPT, it might not be far off. Canva says its in-house AI lab, Canva Research, is “the world’s second most advanced lab for image generation” behind OpenAI. I wanted to find out exactly how Canva’s new AI image generation capabilities compare to ChatGPT’s, so I put the free version of Canva and the free version of ChatGPT head-to-head with five image tests. I gave each tool prompts that were aligned with some of the examples Canva gave in its announcement, like making product photography or blog imagery, and the results are below. Every time Canva creates an image, it presents five options. I chose the first one to make the test fair and presented that on the left of every picture here. With ChatGPT, it tends to make one image, though several times in this test it presented two side-by-side and asked me to pick my favorite to perfect the model. Again, I always went with the first and presented that on the right of every picture below. If you want to know how each AI image generation tool compares, this should be a good starting point for working out which produces the best results and which might be the best option for you. For each prompt I chose a winner based on personal preference, taking into account whether it looked realistic, fit the prompt and whether I could imagine using it in actual design projects. Canva Craft vs. ChatGPT Prompt 1: Product ad image Prompt: Create a polished product photo of a premium silver flip phone on a stone pedestal, with soft studio lighting and a clean beige background. The Canva Craft result is on the left and the ChatGPT result is on the right. (Image credit: Canva / OpenAI) I know some people who use Canva for design mock-ups, especially for ads, websites and social media assets. Which is why I wanted to see how Canva and ChatGPT compare when it comes to creating a realistic-looking product photography. Both Canva and ChatGPT nailed the brief with a very similar interpretation of the prompt. The lighting and textures are certainly believable and have all the hallmarks of a product photoshoot. Of course, if you wanted to use them for a particular product, you’d have to get very specific with the prompt because in these examples these phones clearly don’t exist. Winner: Tied Prompt 2: Desk flat lay Prompt: Create a realistic flat lay of a laptop, notebook, coffee cup, phone, pen and glasses neatly arranged on a wooden desk. The Canva Craft result is on the left and the ChatGPT result is on the right. (Image credit: Canva / OpenAI) I often see people sharing pictures of their desk to add to a LinkedIn post or blog post about the way they work or creativity. A birds eye view of a desk is also a pretty standard image for websites. So I thought this would be a handy test and give us an opportunity to assess the textures and physics of the AI images. Both of the results here looked believable enough to add to a simple blog or social media post. But zoom in and there are some differences. Mostly that the Canva version looks a little less realistic in my opinion due to the angle of the objects and the textures, especially in the coffee. The lighting is a lot more interesting in the Canva version, though the artificial-looking lighting in the ChatGPT image actually makes the scene look more believably office-like. Winner: ChatGPT Prompt 3: Lifestyle photo Prompt: Create a realistic photo of a woman laughing outside a café on a sunny morning, with natural light and a candid editorial feel.…

articles.content: Building a gaming PC is expensive, especially with ongoing price inflation for memory, storage, and graphics cards. Putting together a balanced system with a high-end gaming CPU and a capable graphics card can quickly push budgets beyond what many enthusiasts are willing to spend. If you'd rather skip the hassle of sourcing individual components, we've found a compelling deal on a CyberPowerPC prebuilt gaming desktop, currently available at Best Buy and eBay for $1,749.99. Check out this deal on Best Buy Check out this deal on eBay The prebuilt system is powered by AMD’s Ryzen 7 9800X3D , which is regarded as the gold standard for gaming PCs. This 8-core, 16-thread chip may not be the fastest desktop CPU, but thanks to its 3D V-Cache, it reduces how often your CPU has to fall back on system RAM, drastically improving frame rates while gaming. It also has a modest power draw, making it our pick for the best gaming CPU on the market. The CPU is paired with an AMD B650 M-ATX motherboard that offers built-in Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth, gigabit Ethernet, and multiple USB ports. articles.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
articles.content: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. articles.title: Researchers allege DeepSeek, Kimi, and other Chinese AI models were trained using banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs
articles.content: The topic of U.S. trade controls precluding the export of Nvidia and AMD high-end AI accelerator chips to China has taken a few twists lately. Jensen Huang's affairs aside, it's an open secret in the industry that Nvidia's Blackwell silicon finds its way into China, whether physically or virtually. UnemploymentLabs, an independent research outfit, has come up with strong evidence that those chips were used for training open-weight Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3.1, MiniMax-M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash. The scientists are careful to hedge their findings, noting that while their math checks out, it does not reveal where the chips were, how they were accessed, or prove that export controls were broken. As far as we can tell, it's currently not illegal for Chinese companies to rent Blackwell hardware abroad, and even though Nvidia's grip is tightening , U.S. companies aren't strictly prohibited from doing so, as evidenced by the recent Tencent-Oracle deal . This identification method is limited to models with open weights, and depends on both hardware and software stacks used for model training — and yet it's both clever and simple, like the Egg of Columbus . (Image credit: UnemploymentLabs) Let's establish some base facts. First, different AI accelerator families have unique counts of shader modules (SMs), marginally analogous to CPU cores — Nvidia's Hopper chips have 132, Blackwell B series have 148, and Blackwell GBs come with 152. Second, while there's more than one software stack for training AI models, PyTorch and its CUDA-aware friends are by far the most widely used on the green team's hardware. The first step for training a model is initializing its weights, or how strongly the model considers each individual input. In modern LLM architectures, their initialization goes through a randomization step in which their values are adjusted plus/minus pseudo-randomly, using cuRAND — as in, randomly, but a seed starting value results in the same adjustment figures every time. As you'd expect, doing this for an entire model is a lot of computational work, so this process is spread out across all the SMs, further subdivided into threads. For large weight sets, the thread count per SM is 2,048 for Blackwell and Hopper silicon, and it's surely carefully chosen and optimized for. The researchers repeated a facsimile of the initialization process using the same chips, software, and thread counts. Using relatively simple statistical analysis, they spotted that their final statistical distribution of weight values precisely matched that of DeepSeek, Kimi, et al. As a test, they changed the SM and thread counts, and predictably, the correlation completely broke down. This let them pick out each family of Blackwell/Hopper chip used for each model, and eventually they also figured out an approximate count of cards used. They cannot, however, pinpoint which exact variation produced the weights, as this analysis is linked to initialization layout counts alone, thus SM count and usage pattern — not to VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, or other characteristics that distinguish individual cards. What about AMD cards like the MI300X, or other silicon with a high enough SM count, using the same software stack? The scientists say that it's not impossible that an AMD card could be set up to show up as two groups of 152 or 148 shaders, although we imagine there'd be little reason to do so. Nevertheless, for DeepSeek V4, they also ruled out that possibility by analyzing the actual weight values themselves, and found that AMD cards still didn't produce the same weight value pattern. articles.title: 'Sharp and futuristic': I rode Honda's first full-sized electric motorcycle
articles.content: Up until this point, the electric motorcycle industry has been largely dominated by a brace of brave startups, keen on proving that battery packs and electric motors make the perfect powertrain for a two-wheeler. Maeving has been plowing ahead with its retro-inspired range of excellent city bikes, while Zero has been refining its line of adventure and performance machines for more than 20 years. Harley-Davidson bucked the trend and was arguably the first big-name brand to put its reputation on the line, but sales haven’t exactly been going swimmingly. There are more names to mention, but the sector hasn't yet experienced anywhere near the sort of sales figures that electrified passenger vehicles have. Perhaps it is crying out for a more recognizable brand to get involved? (Image credit: Ed Hill Photography) Now in steps Honda… one of the world’s most recognized automotive brands. After impressing with its CUV e electric scooter , it has decided to take things to the next level and release its first series-production, full-size electric motorcycle in the WN7. This could be just what the market needed. Big bike, big specs (Image credit: Ed Hill Photography) Let’s deal with the name first, because it is, by far, one of the worst things about this machine. The ‘W’ apparently stands for ‘Wind,’ while the ‘N’ represents ‘Naked,’ as in it doesn’t have a fairing. The seven? Well, that’s an indication of where it sits in the lineup, a bit like Kia’s EV naming strategy . As is the way with many electric motorcycles, the WN7 can be specified in two power outputs: an 11kW A1-license-friendly version and an altogether more powerful 18kW version for those with a full A2 license. Of course, licensing regulations differ throughout the world (apologies if you’re reading this from the US), but you get the idea. It can be purchased and ridden by people with a range of experience levels. (Image credit: Ed Hill Photography) Even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration But the quirk of electric motorcycling is that both models have a peak power output of 50kW, or around 67bhp, and a hefty 100Nm of torque. In other words, even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration. The 9.3kWh lithium-ion battery is a 'stressed member', so the big block at the front essentially acts as part of the chassis. For this reason, the batteries aren’t removable, but it looks cool and makes the WN7 handle like a real sport bike. In typical electric motorcycle fashion, there’s no clutch or gear lever to contend with. It’s just a case of twisting the throttle and hanging on. The brakes, thankfully, are laid out like those on a traditional combustion motorcycle, with a lever mounted on the handlebar and a pedal by the right foot that controls the rear brake. (Image credit: Ed Hill Photography) There’s a ‘tank,’ but it’s not filled with fuel. Instead, it houses the charging port, which can handle low-speed home charging as well as DC fast charging at public stations. Honda says that using one of these, a 20% to 80% charge takes around 30 minutes. That’s enough for another 50 miles of riding in the time it takes to stretch the legs and an improvement on what Zero Motorcycles currently offers — although DC fast charging is promised for 2027. Overall, Honda's claimed maximum range is 87 miles on a single charge, but, as you’ll see later, this is a tad unrealistic. A mature ride (Image credit: Ed Hill Photography) Firing up the WN7 is an interesting process. A remote key fob stays in your pocket, while a small ignition button on the frame turns everything on. From there, you pull in the brake lever, press a thumb switch on the handlebar, and it’s ready to go. Cleverly, Honda has added forward and reverse assist, so it’s much easier to maneuver the 217kg machine at low speeds. Holding one of the corresponding buttons and gently twisting the throttle moves the bike backward or forward. As you…

articles.title: Contractor turns a Milwaukee Hackzall into a portable Ethernet untwister after facing job requiring 50,000 custom Cat6 cables
articles.content: A contractor faced a project that required them to create 50,000 custom Cat6 cables from scratch, requiring 100,000 Cat6 terminations. The contractor, who goes by Analytical Horsepower on YouTube , had used a large, rare tool to streamline the job, but afterward he decided to build his own portable tool by modifying a Milwaukee Hackzall, cutting the time to straighten the twisted pairs to under two seconds. His first solution to the problem was to buy a “Wire Straightening Machine” from Alibaba for $500. It does the job well enough, but it’s an industrial machine designed for tabletop use, requiring an AC power source for the power brick and compressed air to run. The concept is that it clamps the wire between two rubber grips using air pressure, and then a linkage converts the rotary motion of the motor into a linear one, allowing the grip to untwist the cable. Since he wanted to use the machine in the field, he needed to make the thing portable — so he disassembled the entire thing, replaced the DC power brick with a 20V DeWalt battery with an adapter, added a push-button switch for power control, and a portable bike pump to deliver compressed air on the go. It worked well at first, but he soon discovered that it was too bulky to use in the tight and hard-to-reach places where Ethernet cables sometimes terminate, like when you’re installing this heavy-duty outdoor Wi-Fi 7 access point . So, he studied the concept — it involved two flat, grippy surfaces grabbing the twisted cables and then moving back and forth. The back-and-forth motion of the surfaces causes the cables to untwist, with the clamping force ensuring that it remains in contact with the cables as they become flatter. With this, he realized that he did not need such a bulky machine to do the job — he just needed a reciprocating tool that could accept a clamp. He first looked at a reciprocating saw, but he found that it still had the same bulky problem and also called it “not overly precise.” But when he looked at the Milwaukee Hackzall, he found that it offered the perfect balance of portability and precision. More importantly, it came with a detailed data sheet, instruction manual, and parts breakdown that allowed him to accurately 3D print the plastic parts and laser-cut and bend the metal parts he needed to build his machine. He also used a toggle clamp to hold the Cat6 cable in place instead of a pneumatic piston, which further simplified the machine and cut its size and weight. After a few steps of trial and error, especially in the quality of the grippy materials used for the clamping surfaces, he finally got it to work. He could reliably untwist softer copper-clad aluminum cables in one go in under two seconds. Harder 100% pure copper conductors, sometimes called solid copper or pure bare copper Ethernet cables, must be untwisted pair-by-pair, though, requiring a bit more time, but it’s still undoubtedly much faster and more convenient than doing the job with just your bare hands. This tool isn’t worth it if you only untwist a few Ethernet cables every month or so, like this telephone-to-gigabit internet conversion job . But if you’re facing a massive job like Analytical Horsepower, that half a minute you save with every cable end could translate to over 830 cumulative hours of labor saved on the jobsite. It’s a great first-generation tool, with its practical use apparent in the YouTube video. Some commenters suggest extending the toggle clamp handle to reach the trigger so activating the tool is easier, while it also looks like a good idea if there’s a way to incorporate the entire system into a crimper.

articles.title: Top Stories: Apple's New Software Approach, iPhone Duo-Optimized Apps, and More
articles.content: Apple's wild past few months are finally starting to slow down with the last of the big hardware launches coming this week. Meanwhile, developers are continuing to optimize their apps for the all-new form factor of the iPhone Duo and Apple looks to shake up its internal iOS and macOS development to give engineers more time to explore and develop new features within the existing update cycles, so read on below for all of the details on these stories and more! Top Stories Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28 Apple has made a change to its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28, and corresponding software updates , according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman. In his Power On newsletter this week, he said Apple separates development of each year's new operating systems into three major stages. Typically, he said each stage consists of four weeks of coding followed by a four-week "convergence" period where new features are integrated into the operating systems. This time around, Apple has made a change, extending the coding period of each stage to six weeks and compressing the convergence period to two weeks, giving engineers more time to come up with and explore ideas before having to lock them in. The change could allow Apple to move more quickly on feature development, part of a general shift toward trying to become more nimble under new CEO John Ternus. 'Apple Support Community' Permanently Closing on November 20 Apple this week abruptly announced that the long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20 . Effective immediately, the Apple Support Community forums are in a read-only state, with new posts no longer being accepted. Longtime members of the community were blindsided by the move and left without an opportunity to post farewell messages to others in the community. Apple Says More Than 100,000 Apps Optimized for iPhone Duo, Here's What's Still Missing Apple last week announced that more than 100,000 apps have been optimized for the iPhone Duo , delivering full compatibility with the device's inner and outer displays. Despite the volume of apps that have been updated, a number of high-profile apps have yet to be optimized, but more and more are being updated each day. The new form factor of the iPhone Duo opens up new possibilities for app functionality and layouts, and we've shared several rounds of fun new apps , innovative games and utilities , and more . Hands-On With Apple's New OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro, HomeView Smart Home Hub, and Apple TV Apple's long-rumored MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now in the hands of customers, and we've shared our initial impressions of Apple's first touchscreen Mac . The touchscreen functionality arrives as part of a new display based on OLED technology, and the machine is significantly lighter than previous models while also delivering a number of other improvements. And yes, the long-lost lighted Apple logo on the lid has made a return! In addition to the new MacBook Pro, we've also gone hands on with the just-launched HomeView smart home hub and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K box . Apple Store Subscription Sign-Up Controversy Exposed In a series of YouTube videos shared over the past few weeks, electronics technician and consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann has exposed a controversy in which some Apple Store employees have allegedly signed up customers for auto-renewing subscription trials for Apple One and other services without their informed consent . Apple has historically tracked the "services attach rate" for retail employees, leading some to feel pressure to push the limits on signing customers up for trials without getting clear permission. Apple has recently removed the attach rate metric for retail employees, though the company has said it is because the metric is less relevant for the holiday season when users are more often buying as gifts rather than for themselves, but the…

articles.title: TikTok Head of Global Security on how SMBs can boost their cybersecurity for free
articles.content: Nearly two-thirds of businesses use social media, and for many smaller firms it’s where customers discover, get to know, and buy from them. This means that for a small or medium-sized business, a social media account is often its shopfront, sales channel, and customer service desk all at once. It pays off. TikTok helped UK small and medium-sized businesses generate an estimated £3.4bn in additional output in 2025. And while a digital-first world can be great for business, scammers and cybercriminals are evolving their tactics to match. In the UK alone, nearly half of small businesses have reported being targeted by a cyber breach or attack. At TikTok, more than 99% of the frauds and scams content we remove is taken down before anyone reports it. But there are plenty of steps businesses should take, and the good news is that it doesn’t require a dedicated tech team or a big budget. 1. Treat unexpected offers as unverified The most effective scams don't look like scams. They look like opportunities: an investor who gets in touch out of the blue, a brand that slides into your DMs with a collaboration but needs an upfront fee to "secure the deal", a service promising to double your followers by Friday. They work because they speak to what every founder wants most: funding and growth. So treat every unexpected offer as unverified until you've checked it yourself, through the organisation's official website or a contact you already trust, never the link or number in the message. And ignore anyone selling likes, followers or verification. At best, you'll get hollow numbers. At worst, you'll hand over the keys to your account. 2. Lock down your logins Your login is the front door to the business you've built. Use a unique password of at least 12 characters for every account your business uses, so one leaked password can't unlock the rest. Turn on 2-Step Verification, so anyone who steals your password still can't get in without a second check. Where your devices support them, set up passkeys. They replace passwords with something tied to your device, like a fingerprint or face scan, which makes them far harder to steal. Finally, never send a password by email or direct message, however urgent the request or familiar the sender. 3. Know who has access In small teams, it's tempting to share one login across everyone: the founder, the part-time social media manager, the freelancer who helped with the launch. It's convenient, but you can't tell who did what, and you can't remove one person without disrupting everyone else. Instead, give each team member their own access, and use a password manager to keep credentials organised. Keep your recovery email and phone number up to date, and check security alerts and active devices regularly. Most importantly, remove employees, freelancers and agencies as soon as their role ends. Offboarding is one of the most overlooked moments in business security, and one of the easiest to get right. 4. Watch what's in shot Behind-the-scenes content, whether that's packing orders or showing how a product is made, is one of the best ways to build a following. It can also give away more than you intend. Before you post, check the background. A delivery label, an order slip or a customer's details left on a packing table can tell a scammer exactly what they need to target you, or the people who buy from you. 5. Report anything suspicious If something feels off, whether it's an email or something you see on social media, report it. Every report helps platforms spot patterns and act faster, protecting not just your business but others being targeted in a similar way. Small habits, serious protection None of these steps requires technical expertise or a dedicated tech team. A cyber incident can be costly, but basic protections cost nothing. Whether you’re a one-person operation or a growing team, these habits will help keep the revenue coming in, and the cybercriminals out. This article was produced as part of…

articles.title: Weeks after shipment was swiped by China, Pentagon ‘struggles to account for’ $31 billion in missing F-35 aircraft parts
articles.content: The Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week. In its report — published just weeks after China purportedly swiped a classified shipment of F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong — the GAO criticized the current inventory system as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.” Possible solutions were also provided by the GAO; however, the implications are that the most advanced and costly fighter jets in U.S. history may not be ready and reliable due to inventory management deficiencies. Inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source. The F-35 program is estimated to cost $1.9 trillion over its lifecycle. It is the most costly weapon system in history, says the GAO. But the Department of Defense (DOD) has “long-standing and ongoing deficiencies related to the accountability and financial reporting of F-35 parts,” asserts the watchdog. Chief among the issues that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts. These are spread among 700 government and contractor facilities worldwide, but the technology for managing massive inventories has existed for decades. We might have seen a telling symptom of the inadequate F-35 parts tracking system back in September. A communications and/or accountability breakdown resulted in a UPS worker routing top-secret parts through Hong Kong to save time. They were allegedly swiped by China after an employee is thought to have missed an email warning not to divert the parts. “Minimal progress” since 2019 Frustratingly, this is the third report since 2019 from the GAO, and the latest published report complains that the DOD has “made minimal progress” in implementing past recommendations. For example, in a 2022 report, periodic physical inventories of F-35 parts were recommended but have not been implemented yet, notes Stars and Stripes . There is also no reliable procedure for verifying data from prime contractors, which can be “inaccurate and incomplete.” Currently, it is believed that there are over 1 million parts, worth more than $85 million, that are lost or missing. Moreover, about 17,000 parts that have been sent in for repair, worth as much as $42.5 billion, aren’t tracked. “Live connection” inventory system Stars and Stripes mentions that the Pentagon is working on “a live connection” for the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO), bridging its inventory software and that of prime contractors with F-35 parts. The JPO asserts that it is now modernizing its infrastructure with direct real-time interfaces. “This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” said a JPO spokesperson, quoted by Breaking Defense .

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
articles.content: Anthropic is positioning its new model , Claude Fable 5.2 , for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates. Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API , it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work. The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input . In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work. The tests I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests: Bug fix : I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed. Code review : I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points. Code writing : The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates. Bug fix Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me). The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s. Astra : 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s. Code review This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table. Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s. Astra : 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s. articles.title: A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?
articles.content: The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running. Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? Too rare Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available. If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? The AI factor AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up. Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited. The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes. The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out. Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland. Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers…

articles.title: Texas residents are complaining about drone noise from Amazon's Prime Air
articles.content: Prime Air drones are attracting noise complaints Houston residents say they're like a 'swarm of bees' Amazon promises the noise pollution is minimal Not for the first time , residents are complaining about the noise coming from Prime Air drones flying over their properties — but Amazon is insisting that the sounds made by their flying machines are "minimal and short-lived". As Chron reports, the people of Houston, Texas are particularly unimpressed with the new aerial delivery service, which started operating in the area earlier this year. The very first Prime Air delivery tests were carried out in 2022. "It was kind of cool and fascinating at first, but now it is driving me crazy," Theresa Gibson, living in the Bridgestone neighborhood, told Chron. "It sounds like a large swarm of bees at a much higher volume than a normal swarm of bees. And it's all day long." According to Gibson, whose home is right in the flight path of the droning drones, dozens of the delivery robots pass overhead every day. A regular stream of noise pollution complaints have been filed by residents since Prime Air moved into the area. Amazon responds Ordering a drone delivery in the Amazon app (Image credit: Amazon) Back in August, Amazon announced that the Prime Air service was expanding to another 500 cities in the US, though operations in the Texas cities Houston, Waco, San Antonio, and Richardson had already been up and running for several months. "During drop-off, the sound level is below that of an idling delivery truck parked curbside and lasts about 30 seconds," Amazon says. "During flight at altitude, it's comparable to a window fan on low and is typically not heard indoors." In a statement given to Chron, Amazon says it's been taking on board feedback. "Our drones spend most of the flight at higher altitudes, and sound heard on the ground is minimal and short-lived, typically lasting about 30 seconds," the statement added. Amazon also said that the general response to its Prime Air drones — and delivery times under 30 minutes — has been "overwhelmingly positive". It's also been meeting with residents and city leaders over changes to flight operations.
articles.author: David Nield
