articles.title: The DreamCloud outperformed several luxury mattresses in our lab tests — and with $599 of free bedding, it’s also the best value deal I’ve seen yet this Black Friday
articles.content: It might still only be mid November but the Black Friday deals are rolling in thick and fast. Case in point: you'll now get $599 worth of free bedding with every mattress at DreamCloud, on top of their 60% off sale. That means you can buy a queen Classic for $699 at DreamCloud , and get two pillows, a sheet set and a mattress protector absolutely free. Despite its mid-range price tag, the DreamCloud Classic is right up there with some of the best mattresses we've tested this year, even out-performing some beds that cost double the price (more on that below). It's an incredibly well-crafted hybrid that we found to be best suited side and back sleepers. DreamCloud mattress sales tend to hold steady throughout the year, which is why this deal is well worth jumping on —$599 worth of free bedding on a mattress of this price is exceptional value for money. If you are still shopping around, we're also tracking the best Black Friday mattress sales from all major brands. Hybrid Mattress (queen): $699 We rate the DreamCloud as the best mattress in a box you can buy, thanks to its luxury finish and mid-range price tag. Our lead tester found its medium-firm tension best suited back and side sleepers, with sturdy edges you can sleep right up to. A $699 queen price is pretty standard, but $599 worth of free bedding is ultra rare — I think this is easily the best value Black Friday deal so far, and I wouldn't wait to shop it. A 365-night night trial and lifetime warranty are included. Our DreamCloud Luxury Hybrid Mattress review score: ★★★★ User score : ★★★★½ (9,200+ reviews) View Deal How the DreamCloud outperformed some luxury rivals in our lab tests In order to test a mattress across key areas, such as motion isolation , temperature regulation and pressure relief , we perform a series of tests in our sleep lab. During our mattress testing process , we found the DreamCloud out-performed some luxury rivals costing double the price in certain areas. For example, the DreamCloud is one of the best hybrid mattresses you can buy online. Its hybrid construction means it has been crafted from a combination of coils and foam comfort layers. (Image credit: Future) When compared to the Bear Elite Hybrid, our top cooling mattress of the year and with a current queen sale price of $1,370, the DreamCloud performed better in our motion isolation and edge support tests, making a compelling argument that the DreamCloud is a better fit for couples. (The Bear is still the better choice for hot sleepers, though). The DreamCloud also performed as well in several key areas, such as edge support, motion isolation and temperature control, as our best mattress for side sleepers , the Helix Midnight Luxe. That's not to say you'll get quite the same level of quality or durable finish with the DreamCloud, but if you're looking for a comfortable mattress for under $1,000 that punches well beyond its mid-range price tag, look no further. Need something firmer? Try this deal instead... Classic Memory Foam (queen): $799 The DreamCloud Classic Hybrid is a medium-firm bed best suited to side and back sleepers, but if you're looking for firmer support, we recommend the memory foam version instead. As well as head-to-toe support, the Classic also boasts a woven fabric cover to wick away moisture and help keep temperatures regulated while you sleep. A queen costs $799 ($100 more than the hybrid). Like the hybrid, it comes with a year's sleep trial and a limited lifetime warranty. articles.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
articles.content: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. articles.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
articles.content: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. articles.title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
articles.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 6, 2025. | Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium's lights. articles.title: How to tell if a Black Friday deal is actually worth it
articles.content: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority I’ve spent the best part of a decade hunting down deals for Android Authority , and I learned very quickly that a big discount doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting a bargain. Black Friday is a particularly good time to remember this, with retailers plastering huge percentage discounts over everything in sight. Contrary to the memes, some are genuinely excellent deals — I can assure you that some tech devices will hit their lowest price ever this month. But you’ll also see many ‘Black Friday deal’ labels on discounts at a price higher than three months ago. Thankfully, there’s a very easy way to tell the difference. The key to assessing a Black Friday deal is to use a price tracker. These tools let you see what a product has cost over recent months or even years, so you can judge for yourself whether that 50% discount is really worth getting excited about. They’re so easy to use that it’ll barely be slowing your shopping spree down at all once you’re in the rhythm. I’ll walk you through it here.

articles.title: I tested Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots, and here’s the one I’m sticking with
articles.content: I’m the first to admit I was late to the game when it came to integrating AI into my life. AI tools on my smartphone felt (and still feel) useless and left a sour taste in my mouth. Large language models I used on my desktop, such as ChatGPT and Claude, showed significantly more promise, but they didn’t feel like something casual users would adopt easily. That’s changed over the last couple of months. I’ve ramped up my Codex usage, and I’ve become interested in chat agents designed to bring powerful AI features and functionality to users who aren’t necessarily up to date on the latest from Anthropic and OpenAI. These new agents are easier to use, look friendlier, and promise to be more proactive.

articles.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Misled Company Leaders On Affair With Chinese Businesswoman
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang misled several of the company's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters. [...] During the autumn of 2025 and in October 2026, in response to press queries that drew some Nvidia leaders' attention to his relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Huang at both times described their interactions as appropriate, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Reuters only reviewed messages from the exchanges in October, not the ones from 2025. In two separate messages in October, Huang told Nvidia leaders, including Teter and Wagonfeld, that the interactions reflected standard business dealings with customers. In other messages, Huang affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed. Nvidia's Huang also discussed taking legal action against the New York Times after it published an article in October of last year that drew attention to his meetings in public with Alice Huang, the people said. That article had prompted Jensen Huang to communicate with some Nvidia leaders in 2025 about their interactions, which he did not describe as an affair, the people said. Ultimately, neither Nvidia nor Huang filed a lawsuit against the paper. A spokesperson for the New York Times said the paper received no legal demand. It is unclear when his relationship with Alice Huang became intimate. Photos posted online and verified by Reuters show them together in the US, China and elsewhere, dating as far back as December 2023. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.fingerprint: affair businesswoman ceo chinese company leaders misled nvidia

articles.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
articles.content: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®
articles.author: Richard Speed

articles.title: Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs
articles.content: Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder ( Qwen3-Embedding-4B ) and decoder ( Qwen3-8B ) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at…

articles.title: 5 apps you can use instead of Google Messages
articles.content: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority Google Messages is easily one of the best messaging apps for Android, and RCS support is a large part of the reason. While Samsung used to support RCS directly, these days the only true RCS solution for Android is Google’s official app. As much as RCS has improved Android messaging, I understand that not everyone has bought into the standard. If you’re not concerned about RCS support, there are plenty of other great messaging apps out there as well. Let’s take a look at a few of the best messaging apps out there. To keep things interesting, we’ll take a look at both SMS-based apps and those that use proprietary formats via the web.
articles.author: Andrew Grush

articles.title: Don’t buy the new Apple TV 4K until Apple does these 3 things
articles.content: I’m a huge fan of Apple’s digital media player, the Apple TV 4K. I’ve owned every version of the Apple TV for over a decade now, and have used Apple’s Movies store to purchase hundreds of films. The diminutive Apple TV 4K is my sole portal to my television, and it easily beats other media streamers—including those from Roku, Amazon, and Google—when it comes to ease of use and user interface. Like many, I had been eagerly waiting for a new Apple TV 4K, ready to upgrade. Apple’s last version came out back in 2022, and though it still works perfectly fine, I was excited to see what new modern features and improvements the 2026 model would have. But the 2026 model, which went on sale on Friday, November 13—it kills me to say—is a letdown. The hardware is fantastic, but the device is failed by its software. And its price is double that of its predecessor. For the first time since I began buying Apple TVs more than a decade ago, I’ll be sitting this model out—and you probably should, too—until Apple does these three things. Fixes its TV app The worst thing about the Apple TV, ironically, has always been its TV app. That’s the app you use to access the Apple TV streaming service, as well as all the movies and TV shows you’ve purchased from the iTunes Store. I’ve written in detail about the TV app before, and unfortunately its weakness remains, even in tvOS 27, the operating system that powers the new Apple TV 4K. It’s so barebones that it feels like the development team behind it created it as an afterthought. The actual video playback of the TV app is fine. It’s got a nice Liquid Glass sheen and is pretty fluid. But it’s also, ostensibly, designed to be the home for all your digital entertainment—how you access all the movies and series you’ve purchased through the iTunes Store. And it’s horrible at that. The most egregious failure (and there are many ) of the TV app is that it still doesn’t offer the basic functionality of letting users organize their purchased movies and series into collections for easy categorization on the Apple TV 4K. And this is sorely needed, because the built-in Genre categories the app does offer so often misclassify or outright omit movies that it seems like a sin against cinema itself. Adds missing apps A second frustration with the Apple TV 4K is that it is still lacking two apps all other Apple devices support—and these apps are perfect for a television. One is a dedicated Home app, as you have on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even the Apple Watch. Apple positions the Apple TV 4K as one of the central hubs of your smart home, so it’s baffling that the company hasn’t ported its Home app to it, which would let you monitor and control your security feeds and smart devices from the comfort of your couch. Then there is the Weather app. Apple’s Weather app is the most beautiful out there, thanks to rich graphics that visually represent local conditions. And, you know, for some 70 years now, people have been conditioned to tune into their TVs to get their local weather forecast. So why does the Apple TV, after all these years, still not have a dedicated Weather app that you can access with a click of the Siri Remote? Expands its gaming capabilities In advance of the new Apple TV 4K announcement, many people, including myself , speculated (and indeed, hoped) that Apple would finally turn the Apple TV 4K into a true gaming console. But when Apple released the new unit, with the powerful A19 chip inside, the company didn’t announce any new gaming capabilities to go with it. This was surprising, since the new A19 chip is more than capable of running AAA console games, unlike the A15 chip in the prior-generation Apple TV 4K. I mean, even the A17 Pro chip in the iPhone 15 Pro, which is inferior to the A19, can run AAA titles like the Resident Evil 2 remake, Assassin’s Creed Mirage , Red Dead Redemption , Control: Ultimate Edition , Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas , and more. Of all these gripes, the new Apple TV…
articles.author: Michael Grothaus

articles.title: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
articles.content: Runway releases its robotics model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The model uses knowledge from video training for robot control and leads the World Action Model category on Nvidia's RoboLab-120 benchmark. It can't yet plan complex action sequences on its own, though. The article Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: The new Siri is so far behind the competition it could bring down Apple — here’s why
articles.content: We posted two reviews of new Apple products this week in the Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K , and there was one common theme. Apple’s Siri AI still isn’t good enough. In fact, I’d argue that there’s still such a large gap between Siri and other AI assistants like Gemini, ChatGPT, Alexa+ and Muse that people could start to defect to other brands if Apple doesn’t get its act together. And soon. HomeView needs help (Image credit: Future) For example, my colleague Mike Prospero compared the new HomeView against Amazon’s Echo Show 8 with Alexa+, and he found that Apple’s assistant isn’t nearly as capable. Mike could easily order a pizza through Uber Eats with Amazon’s device while Apple’s Siri just offered to make a call. Siri is not the AI agent you’ve been looking for. Meanwhile, Engadget pointed out that Siri AI gets dumber the moment your iPhone is not within range. It defaults to generic world-knowledge answers. And Joanna Stern noted in her review that Siri stumbled on multi-step household tasks and at one point refused to open her front door despite recognizing her face. It also didn’t help that the HomeView Siri started “talking” to other phone-based Siris in the house. (Image credit: Apple) To be clear, Siri AI has improved versus previous versions, but it’s still quite limited as an everyday assistant compared to Google Gemini, Alexa+, ChatGPT, and Muse. And I’d argue that the longer Siri continues to lag, the more Apple is leaving the door open for competitors to overtake Apple. Apple TV + Siri = Meh (Image credit: Future) Apple Intelligence, such as it is, also graces the new Apple TV 4K, a streaming device that costs a whopping $299. Apple is justifying the premium partly by touting the fact that Siri is inside, which is supposed to help you find things to watch. But things didn’t go very well in our testing. When Mike asked Siri to find scary movies for kids, Siri first responded “I’m not finding anything for that.” Then on the second attempt asking for scary movies good for kids the recommendations were nightmare fuel like “Poltergeist,” “Alien,” and “Seven.” Meanwhile, the Google TV Streamer and Fire TV returned recommendations like “Coraline,” “Goosebumps 2,” “Hocus Pocus,” and “The Addams Family.” Asking “What’s that movie with Audrey Hepburn that takes place in Rome” resulted in a bunch of Christmas movies, none with Hepburn. Though, Siri AI performed better with Tom Hanks action flicks. Siri AI on iPhone still limited (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) Apple’s assistant has gotten better on the iPhone, especially with personal context. For example, I asked Siri AI to find the message from my daughter asking about earrings as a gift. You can also perform multiple actions at once using your voice. I recently had it look up restaurants around Bryant Park that are rated 4 stars or higher but under $50 for lunch and then craft an outgoing message that includes the address for each and top dish. It worked seamlessly. However, Siri AI is still missing two big things versus other assistants: live voice chat with video and powerful agentic features. It’s not a good sign that I’ve now mapped Gemini Live to the Action button on my iPhone 17 Pro Max . That’s because I use Google’s voice assistant in combination with live video all of the time to ask questions and troubleshoot things around the house. For example, I was able to fix a cantilever umbrella because Gemini could see what I was talking about and offer advice in real time. With Siri AI, you can share what’s on your screen but not a live video feed. It’s getting to the point where I wish I could say “Hey, Gemini” to my iPhone. Agentic AI is still in a nascent stage, but this is yet another area where Siri is still behind. In fact, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman recently reported that new CEO John Ternus has explicitly asked for the Siri AI team to speed things up here. Right now you just can’t do things like book an Uber with Siri or perform complex tasks…
articles.author: Mark Spoonauer

articles.title: KitchenAid vs. Ooni: I tested both stand mixers — here is what I'm keeping
articles.content: KitchenAid Artisan Plus The KitchenAid Artisan Plus has a 5-quart bowl, and comes in an array of colorways. Ooni Halo Core The Oon Halo Core has a 4.8 quart bowl and comes in either White or Black. KitchenAid is famous for making some of the best stand mixers on the market. As a home writer who tests a mountain of kitchen appliances, it’s one of the few brands I know I can consistently rely on. I recently tested one of its newest models, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus , and no surprises, I love it. But straight after giving it a glowing 5-star rating, the Ooni Halo Core spiral stand mixer landed in my kitchen. While the price tag on both appliances makes my eyes water, I’m wasn't sure what to expect from a brand best known for pizza ovens . Could Ooni really rival KitchenAid? Both are excellent mixers, and I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend them — but which one is the standout winner? KitchenAid Artisan Plus vs Ooni Halo Core: Price (Image credit: Future / Camilla Sharman) A good benchmark when comparing products is the price. Usually, you can weigh the pros and cons of each appliance and then decide whether the more expensive product is worth the upgrade. But it’s a bit tricky with these two stand mixers, since they hit the same price point — unless you find one on sale. The KitchenAid Artisan Plus is $599 at Crate & Barrel , although certain colorways are reduced to $429 , including Mint Juelp, Steel Blue and Oat. Ooni’s Halo Core Spiral Dough Mixer is also $599 at Amazon, although it only holds the Foundry Black Colorway. However, you can pick the Polar White colorway directly from Ooni or Williams Sonoma. Winner: Draw KitchenAid Artisan Plus vs Ooni Halo Core: Design (Image credit: Future / Camilla Sharman) These two mixers are at opposite ends of the spectrum when it comes to design. Ooni offers a much more contemporary style appliance, and its overall aesthetic gives the impression that it means business. It wouldn’t look out of place in a professional kitchen, similar to its big brother, the Halo Pro Spiral stand mixer , which will set you back $799 at Amazon , an extra $200 if you’d prefer the upgrade. From testing these stand mixers, they both mean business and are sturdy, reliable appliances, but if you’re looking for an appliance to stay out permanently on your countertop, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus would be my choice — though my interior style is more modern cottage than modern urban. And if color is your thing, picking a KitchenAid is a no-brainer! Winner: KitchenAid KitchenAid Artisan Plus vs Ooni Halo Core: Functions (Image credit: Future / Camilla Sharman) These mixers both do the same thing—they can beat, whisk and knead —but the Ooni Halo Core is designed with dough in mind. Although it’s still adept at mixing cakes and whisking (it has a double whisk), it really shines at mixing and kneading dough. While the KitchenAid has a standard dough hook, the Ooni takes it a step further by including a breaker bar. This dual-kneading design develops stronger gluten networks in your dough — perfect if you like to bake homemade pizza in one of Ooni’s pizza ovens. You can see in the above photo how the breaker bar sits centrally in the mixing bowl, and a spiral pattern is made within the dough. The bowl shield also has a handy feed that ensures that any liquids hit the central point and get quickly incorporated into the mix. (Image credit: Future / Camilla Sharman) Although both machines can knead a lot of dough, I found the Ooni sat slightly above the KitchenAid in terms of power, but don’t let that put you off buying a KitchenAid if you want to make bread — it’s still an exceptional machine. (Image credit: Future / Camilla Sharman) The KitchenAid is an excellent all-rounder, and apart from kneading dough without shifting on your countertop, it beats and whips to perfection. I found that the shaped bowl and double flex-edge beater mean that there’s hardly a morsel of cake batter left on the side of the bowl, and you don’t…

articles.title: I thought Breath of the Wild ruined classic Zelda for me, then I played Ocarina of Time on Nintendo Switch 2 — and I was very wrong
articles.content: In February 2021, I wrote an op-ed titled “Breath of the Wild ruined traditional Zelda for me.” Back then, I mused that Breath of the Wild being my first-ever Zelda game had made going back to the older titles in the beloved Nintendo franchise difficult. Flash-forward to now, and I’m roughly halfway through the new Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2 , and I’m loving it. I’ll cut my past self a little slack. February 2021 was more than five years ago, and a person’s tastes can change a lot in that amount of time. Heck, in those days, I also thought Souls games weren’t for me. Now in 2026, I’ve beaten every modern title FromSoftware has released (bar Dark Souls 2 ; it’s in my overflowing backlog) and am basically obsessed with the Soulslike genre. Nevertheless, I definitely wrote off classic Zelda games too hastily. Turns out all it took was pretty much the most acclaimed video game of all time getting a stunning remake for me to see just how foolish I had been. Consider this follow-up article my formal apology to Link. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2, and in a word, it's stunning. This complete remake of the classic Nintendo 64 offers overhauled visuals, improved controls, and a few smart tweaks to make the timeless game even more modern. Ocarina of Time was considered a masterpiece back in 1998, and this new version on Switch 2 has earned the same plaudits. View Deal Turns out proper Zelda dungeons are delightful Ocarina of Time starts a little slow. Lots of text boxes and simple tutorials. But once the adventure really begins, and Young Link is tasked with finding three Spiritual Stones (the first is obtained during the prologue chapter), I started to discover exactly why longtime fans bemoan Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom ’s lack of “proper” Zelda dungeons. But it was only once I had obtained all three stones and transformed into grown-up Link that I really understood what makes these dungeons so special, and why fans still beg for the series to bring them back. Nintendo’s penchant for creative and satisfying puzzles is on full display in the Forest, Fire and Water Temple, and I’m very excited to head to the remaining dungeons and discover what’s hiding within their twisting corridors. The Fire Temple is a great example of phenomenal design, as the underground lava-laden cavern loops back on itself in surprising and creative ways. The infamous Water Temple might actually be my frontrunner favorite, probably because the remake has stripped away the friction of the original. (Image credit: Nintendo) Best of all is the way each dungeon gives you a new tool to play with, which is then vital to unlocking the dungeon’s many secrets; it is a consistently brilliant way of asking players to make use of their entire arsenal of tools. My favorite aspect of Breath of the Wild (and sequel Tears of the Kingdom ) has always been the puzzle shrines. While it’s not an original opinion, the dungeons in Ocarina of Time feel like a couple dozen BOTW puzzle shrines stitched together in an environmentally cohesive manner. Delving into a dungeon feels appropriately epic, and each one (or at least, each one I’ve experienced so far) begs to be fully explored with treasure chests and secrets for those willing to look in every corner. They’re just a blast, and yes, I can finally admit, they flow better than Breath of the Wild’s pretty repetitive Divine Beast dungeons. Mixing new and old could make for the perfect Zelda game (Image credit: Nintendo) While I’ve at long last come around to the strengths of the traditional Zelda formula, that doesn’t mean I’ve suddenly lost my intense love for Breath of the Wild and its own acclaimed formula. Sorry, Ocarina stans, but Link’s 2017 adventure remains my favorite game in the series (of the ones I’ve played). If there is one element where Ocarina of Time can’t compete with Breath of the Wild, it’s in the latter's ability to let you…

articles.title: I tested the world’s largest flat super ultrawide monitor that’s like have two 27-inch screens side by side — and it’s a game changer for multitasking
articles.content: The Innocn E49M1R isn’t your standard super ultrawide monitor. Instead of a curved panel like on other popular massive displays, it’s completely flat and gives you the screen real estate of two 27-inch, 1440p monitors running across your desk. When connected to your PC or Mac, you can have two full-sized browser windows or apps running side by side. This makes the E49M1R an excellent choice for productivity, though with a 165Hz panel, Mini-LED backlighting, and AMD FreeSync Premium, it also provides a very immersive gaming experience — granted you have a PC powerful enough to run games at this monitor’s native resolution. I’ve been using the E49M1R as my daily driver for a month now, and it’s definitely changed how I work. While I’ve used a standard 21:9 ultrawide display for almost a decade, jumping to 32:9 and all that extra screen space has made a real difference while multitasking. Still, it has its trade-offs. While this monitor offers dual HDMI and DisplayPort connections, it’s missing a USB-C port for a one-cable connection to your laptop. Likewise, due to its VA panel and sheer width, colors can appear washed out at the edges if you’re sitting too close. My Innocn E49M1R review will help you decide if this is the best monitor for your workflow and your desk, or if it’s worth going with something smaller or slightly curved instead. Innocn E49M1R: Cheat Sheet What is it? A massive 49-inch, Mini-LED super ultrawide monitor that’s flat instead of curved. Who is it for? Those who prefer flat displays over curved ones and want a very wide screen for productivity-focused work or gaming. What does it cost? The Innocn E49M1R costs $999 but is currently on sale for $849 at Amazon and on the company’s site. What do we like? The Mini-LED backlighting, the generous port selection, its impressive SDR and HDR brightness, and that it’s the widest flat super ultrawide monitor available. What don’t we like? That content at the edges looks washed out due to its size and VA panel, and the lack of a USB-C port for easily connecting a laptop. Innocn E49M1R: Specs Price $999 Display 49 inches Resolution 5120 x 1440 Aspect ratio 32:9 Refresh rate 165 Hz Response time 8ms Adaptive sync AMD FreeSync Premium Panel type VA Backlight Mini-LED Local dimming zones 1760 HDR HDR 1000 Color depth 8-bit DPI 109 PPI Inputs 2 x HDMI 2.1, 2 x DisplayPort 1.4, 1 x audio out, 2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-B Speakers 2 x 5W VESA 100 x 100mm Dimensions 47.82 × 1.99 × 14.43 inches (without stand), 47.82 × 9.31 × 21.44 inches (with stand) Weight 29.32 pounds with stand (13.3kg) Warranty 1-year Innocn E49M1R: The Ups The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, as there’s no other flat super ultrawide display this large. It takes up the full width of most desks, but in return, you get an impressively bright picture, plenty of screen real estate, enough input ports to connect four devices at once, and built-in speakers for the complete package. A massive (yet flat) display (Image credit: Tom's Guide) At 47.82 x 1.99 x 14.43 inches, the E49M1R is the largest monitor I’ve ever unboxed. Just like with a large TV, I’d recommend having someone help you unpack it and install the included metal stand. In addition, you also get a power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a DisplayPort cable in the box. Unfortunately, there isn’t a USB-B cable included, which you’ll need if you want to take advantage of the E49M1R’s built-in USB hub — more on that later. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Just like with the other Innocn monitors I’ve tested, installing the metal stand is a breeze. It simply snaps into the back of the monitor, and a single thumb screw attaches the arm to its sturdy metal base. If you’d rather use one of the best monitor arms instead of the included stand, there are 100 x 100 VESA mounting holes on the back of the display. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) One thing I really appreciate about the E49M1R is that instead of tucking all the ports on the underside like you often see on other…

articles.title: Ready for your next getaway? I use these 7 ChatGPT plugins to find the best local tours, organize an existing itinerary and more before I travel
articles.content: There’s a list of things that bring equal levels of excitement and stress with them: moving to a new place, starting your own business and going on a first date are among those activities. For me, setting up everything I need to enjoy a future vacation is also on that list. The months of preparation that go into ensuring my flight plans, hotel stay and getaway plans go off with as few problems as possible are nerve-racking. I’ve watched my parents get headaches from just trying to plan a family trip to Disney World , so I’ve been trying to lessen the amount of stress that comes with that sort of thing now that I do it. There are plenty of AI tools that are specifically made to help people plan their big trips. For me, I’ve gotten a lot out of ChatGPT’s plugins since there are a good number of them that are tailor-made for vacation planning. If you want some extra assistance during your preparation period for domestic and international excursions, be like me and use the following plugins & associated prompts to make your future vacation even better. 1. Only include tours with a traveler rating of at least 4 out of 5 and a duration strictly under three hours. Prioritize tours with confirmed departures that start and finish during daylight hours, [name of location] local time. Show each tour’s rating, review count, duration and daytime departure options where available. Flag any unconfirmed schedule details. If fewer than 10 tours meet these requirements, return fewer. 2. Tripsy (Image credit: Shutterstock) Connecting your Tripsy account to ChatGPT via this plugin lets you manage your trip a whole lot easier. Some of the best uses that come from utilizing this plugin include summarizing your vacation plans, finding any gaps in your itinerary that could be filled with an activity, bringing up crucial reservation details you’ve been desperately searching for, etc. If you have any itineraries, reservations, activities or any other vacation details attached to your Tripsy, it’s worth using any of the following prompts to command ChatGPT to interact with them: Turn my [trip name] reservations into a day-by-day itinerary. Include local departure times, addresses, and gaps between activities. Review my saved [destination] itinerary for overlapping reservations, tight connections, and missing details. Rank the issues I should resolve first. Summarize tomorrow’s plans from Tripsy into a travel briefing: where I need to be, when to leave, confirmation details available, and anything I still need to arrange. 3. articles.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
articles.content: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if…

articles.title: Shadow AI in the Workplace: Data Security Risks and Governance Strategies
articles.content: It is 1:45 AM. A junior associate is sitting at their desk, trying to finish a 110-page agreement that has to be ready by 8:00 AM. The coffee has gone cold. After hours of reading the same pages, even simple clauses are becoming difficult to understand. There is still a lot of work left, and very little time. The associate opens a free AI chatbot on a personal phone and copies three clauses from the agreement. Within seconds, the tool provides a short summary. The work becomes a little easier, and the associate moves on to the next task. But there is one problem. The law firm has already banned the use of public AI tools. Its computers block access to these websites, and employees have been warned not to use them for professional work. Yet the associate has found another way to access the same tool through a personal device. The firm's system may show that its restrictions are working. But it cannot necessarily show what the associate has shared through a personal connection. This is one way Shadow AI can enter a workplace. The employee may not intend to expose confidential information. They may simply be trying to finish an urgent task. But the information has still moved outside the organisation's control. And this raises a question that companies need to consider: If employees are still finding ways to use AI despite a workplace ban, is blocking access really enough to protect the organisation? Understanding the Shadow AI Problem Shadow AI refers to the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without the knowledge or approval of their organisation. These tools may include public chatbots, AI writing assistants, browser extensions, coding tools and meeting transcription applications. The problem is not limited to which tool an employee uses. It is also about what information they share with it. An employee may upload a client document to get a summary, enter company data to prepare a report, or share a section of source code to find an error. These actions may appear harmless from the employee's point of view. However, the organisation may have no clear understanding of where that information goes, how it is stored or what happens to it after the task is completed. Many companies have responded by restricting or blocking public AI platforms. Their concerns are understandable. Confidential information, customer records and business documents should not be shared with services that have not been properly assessed. However, a restriction does not automatically change employee behaviour. If a company blocks an AI website but continues to expect employees to complete the same workload within the same deadlines, the reason for using AI does not disappear. Some employees may simply find another way to access it. This is where the real problem begins. A company may successfully block an application on its office network while remaining unaware that employees are using the same application through personal phones, private accounts or other connections. Banning AI may restrict access through official systems, but it does not necessarily stop its use. In some situations, it can move that use beyond the organisation's visibility. Why Employees Bring Their Own AI Tools The use of AI at work is growing faster than many organisations can introduce their own systems and policies. Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index reported that 75% of global knowledge workers were using AI at work. Among those using AI, 78% were bringing their own AI tools to work, commonly described as Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI). This pattern aligns with broader enterprise trends. Research from Gartner shows that over 41% of employees actively acquire, modify, or use technology outside the visibility of IT department. These figures are important because they show that employees are not waiting for their organisations to introduce every tool they want to use. But they should be understood carefully: they show workplace AI adoption and the use of…

articles.title: Vercel Releases UI SDK: 50+ UI Behaviors for AI Coding Agents
articles.content: Vercel Labs has released UI SDK , an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 50+ behaviors, 51 component modules in the repo, 6 npm packages at 0.1.0-beta.1 Runs on: Any modern browser, no GPU. React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC, or plain Web Components Performance: In Vercel’s own test, an agent used 69% fewer tool calls on a settings task Best: Task time fell 61%, from 41 s to 16 s, with the agent bridge (self-reported) Worst: That benchmark covers 1 task and 3 runs, and beta APIs may still change What is Vercel UI SDK? UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core . Thin adapters render it in each framework. The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet. How does UI SDK work? Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive . A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery . Its Clear button appears only when there is text. Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts . The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Which behaviors ship? Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include: createRovingFocus : arrow keys move through a list with 1 Tab stop createTypeahead : type a few letters to jump to an item createPopup : opens next to its trigger and stays on screen createSelection : select 1 or many, with Shift and Ctrl createReorder , createResize , createViewport and createVirtualizer The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. How do agents learn it? Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent . It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md . That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk . Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing . Can agents operate the UI directly? Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue . Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP. UI SDK benchmark: agent bridge vs browser tools Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs . Metric Browser tools UI SDK + bridge Change Tool calls 16 5 -69% Text read (characters) 39.8k 6.8k -83% Time 41 s 16 s -61% Cost $0.073 $0.032 -56% Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version. articles.title: This simple QR code creator is all about your privacy
articles.content: QR codes are popping up everywhere these days, and for good reason. They have all kinds of practical uses, from replacing your business card and collecting cashless payments to linking to menus or information on museum exhibits. But creating one can be a pain. Search online for “QR code creator,” and you’ll run into sluggish websites with annoying banner ads, sign-up walls, and invasive privacy policies. Some even hijack your links with their own tracking code. It really shouldn’t be this complicated. Fortunately, today’s tool introduces a new way to create QR codes that’s refreshingly simple—and it comes from a source with a strong track record of keeping your data private. This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence . Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures! The simplest QR code creator A little refresher before getting to the tool itself: QR codes are those square-shaped barcodes full of little pixelated squares and a set of larger markers in the corners. You might see them in restaurants (“Leave us a review on Yelp!”), from street vendors collecting Venmo payments, or as part of the setup process for a smart home device. Most of the time, scanning them just opens a link to a web page without your having to type anything. ➜ For a simple, straightforward way to create your own QR codes with ease, check out Ente QR , a free website with no sign-ups or usage limits. ⌚ Generating a code takes mere seconds , and only a few minutes longer if you want to customize the look. Ente QR makes QR code creation as quick and easy as it should be. There are any number of reasons why you might find it helpful to create QR codes of your own. I keep an image file with a QR code handy on my phone, for instance, to let folks easily sign up for my newsletters. You could also have a QR code that links to your website on business cards, a printout of one that points people to a shared digital photo album for your next party, or to a page with your Wi-Fi password and other details for house guests. ✅ Whatever you want to use it for, Ente QR lets you create a code with a few simple steps: Paste a link into the address field. Tweak the color and visual style of the QR code. Click the download button to get the QR code image as a PNG image file. The site’s customization features strike the right balance between simplicity and utility, with a handful of dot formatting options and preset colors, plus a color picker if you want something specific. There’s also a “Logo” option that embeds an image in the middle of the QR code. Ente’s tool is the perfect mix of simplicity and function. Ente says the QR code creation runs entirely in your browser, and the codes always lead directly to the link you included, with no creepy tracking in between. It’s a side project from a company that mainly works on private photo and document storage. The biggest limitation is that Ente’s QR codes are only for linking to web addresses. If you want to create a QR code for sharing plain text, a prefilled email, or a digital contact card, BlockSurvey’s privacy-focused QR code generator is a good alternative. While it’s not as stylish as Ente QR, it supports more data formats—but for most people’s purposes, Ente more than fits the bill. Ente QR is available in any browser and works well on both desktop and mobile devices. It’s free to use with no ads, sign-ups, subscriptions, or usage limits. Ente does not track the URLs in the QR codes you create and does not set tracking cookies on its website. Treat yourself to all sorts of brain-boosting goodies like this with the free Cool Tools newsletter —starting with an instant introduction to an incredible audio app that’ll tune up your days in truly delightful ways.

articles.title: How I Built an AI Marketing Team With Grok Bot Without Writing Code
articles.content: A non-engineer’s notes on running marketing with Grok Bot: one job per bot, a rules file every job reads, and nothing goes out without me Last time I wrote about building a consumer mobile app on nights and weekends with AI coding agents. The code was only half the problem. An app nobody hears about is a hobby. And I don’t have a marketing team. So I built one out of bots. I use Grok Bot, where each bot has its own computer and can run jobs on a schedule. Here’s how it’s set up and what I’ve learned so far. One bot, one job My first instinct was one big assistant that does everything. That’s like hiring one rep to prospect, run demos, do legal, and forecast. Nothing gets done well. So every bot gets one job, written at the top of its instructions. The marketing bot owns content ideas. Every weekday morning it pitches a few ranked ideas for short-form video and carousel posts, recommends one to make today, and drafts it when I say go. The chief of staff bot checks the other bots every weekday before 8am. It reads what they actually produced, not what they say they did, and marks each one on track, slipping, or stalled. A bot that designs bots. When I need a new one, I describe the job and it writes the instructions: one job, one voice, and a list of things the bot must never do. That last list matters more than the job itself. It’s the same lesson from coding agents. An agent with no boundaries will happily do things you never asked for. Draft only. I hit post. The marketing bot never posts, comments, or messages anyone. It drafts. I post. That one rule removes most of the risk. A bad draft costs me thirty seconds. A bad post under my name costs a lot more. It’s approval tiers again. A rep can draft the proposal. They can’t sign the contract. A rules file every job reads first The marketing bot has one rules file, and every job reads it before doing anything. It holds the guardrails and a lessons section. The guardrails are short: No spending. No ads, no paid tools, no paid creators. Never invent quotes, stats, or customers. Every quote gets a link and a date. Check factual claims against a real source. Only make product claims that are true today. Then once a week, the Friday report adds a few plain lessons to the bottom. These are real ones from the first week: We couldn’t count signups, because there’s no signup page yet. So signups stay “unknown,” never a guess. Check every post about an hour after it goes up. One post sat at zero views and nobody noticed. Log every post the same day it goes up. Two posts were only found later. Then I changed the goal. Since there’s no signup page, posts stopped asking people to sign up. Now they close on a follow or a comment prompt. The bot wrote that change into the same file, with the date, so every job picks it up the next morning. If you read my last piece, this will sound familiar. It’s the same idea as the instruction file for my coding agent. If a decision only lives in a chat, the next run won’t know about it. Batch the work Early on, the marketing bot built a content bank: 21 days of posts, planned out, so I’m never starting from a blank page. That’s the real win for me. Not that the bot is creative. That I don’t have to decide what to post every single day. I review a plan, say yes or no, and move on. A manager for the bots Bots drift. They’ll report “done” on things that half-happened. So the chief of staff bot doesn’t trust the reports. It reads the actual output. If a bot is off track, it nudges that bot once with the goal, what’s missing, and the next step. If it’s still off the next day, it flags it to me. Its rules say never invent progress or metrics, and mark anything it can’t verify as unverified. I want a pipeline review, not a happy-ears forecast. What I’d tell another non-engineer You don’t need a marketing team to start. You need a few narrow bots and a way to catch them when they’re wrong. For me that’s four things. One job per bot. A list of things each bot must…

articles.title: How to Watch the Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order
articles.content: So, full disclosure, I don’t really believe in watching movies in chronological order the first time around. I think that watching them by release date is usually the best way to go. However, if you’re planning on doing it for the Hunger Games movies, I’ve got you covered. Here are all the Hunger Games movies in chronological order. Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping The Hunger Games The Hunger Games: Catching Fire The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1 The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2 1. The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes The first movie in the Hunger Games’ timeline, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes sees a young Coriolanus Snow trying to navigate the craziness that is the country of Panem. He eventually finds himself actively involved in the 10th annual Hunger Games as a mentor for District 12’s female tribute, Lucy Gray Baird. Snow wants to be on top of the world, which means he’ll do anything and everything to see his dream realized. Cheat, kill, backstab - nothing is off limits if it means inching closer and closer to the top. 2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Set 40 years after the events of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, it focuses on District 12 male tribute Haymitch Abernathy as he is forced to compete in the 50th Hunger Games. This time, though, the rules have changed. Every 25th Hunger Games, a new concept is added to make that year’s game even more special. So, for the 50th Hunger Games, they decide to double the number of tributes. 48 in total, 4 from each district. It’s hard enough to win a normal Hunger Games, but to do it with double the people is damn near impossible. Haymitch will have to overcome the overwhelming odds if he wants to survive. 3. The Hunger Games Fast forward 24 years, and we arrive at the 74th Hunger Games. Yes, the Hunger Games are still going, but the 12 Districts that are forced to send their children to death every year are sick and tired of it all. Revolution is coming. All it needs is for someone to light the fire. In the midst of all this, District 12 teenager Katniss Everdeen volunteers to participate in the Hunger Games in place of her little sister. Alongside District 12 male tribute Peeta Mellark, Katniss will have to train and learn the inner workings of the games to outlast the other tributes and make it back home to her family. 4. The Hunger Games: Catching Fire The fire of rebellion is spreading, and the government of Panem knows that it has to do something before it spreads too far. Katniss, who survived last year’s games, is seen as a dangerous individual who’s fanning the flames. President Snow decides that something has to be done about her and the other former Hunger Games victors. For the 75th Hunger Games, a new special concept is added. Katniss and 23 other former Hunger Games winners will return to compete to the death. Knowing that they’re beloved by the populace, they tug at their heartstrings to try and get out of the games, further pushing people to revolt. 5. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1 The rebellion is in full swing following the games, and Katniss, whether she wants to or not, is seen as the face of it. Most of the districts are quick to join her side, but President Snow won’t go quietly into that good night. He still has a few tricks up his sleeve, including brainwashing someone who’s very close to Katniss. I can’t go into more detail without spoiling the movie, but this is where things get serious. And they only get more serious in the following and final movie. 6. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2 The war between the rebellion and President Snow is finally coming to an end. All the districts are united against him; the only thing left to do is to storm the Capitol and to take down the president himself. But President Snow refuses to lose gracefully. Throughout the city, he has laid out traps for Katniss…

articles.title: How to Evaluate Snowflake Cortex Embedding Models for Enterprise Search
articles.content: Picture this. A company has 500,000 support tickets sitting in Snowflake. Years of troubleshooting notes, product defects, workarounds, resolutions, and occasional messages that just say "fixed after restart." Very helpful, thanks. Someone wants an AI assistant that can search those tickets and suggest resolutions. The architecture looks straightforward. Take the documents, generate embeddings, store vectors, retrieve similar records, and let an LLM write the answer. A few SQL queries later, you have a demo. Then someone asks which embedding model you picked. "Arctic." Which Arctic? "The bigger one." Why? "More dimensions." And there it is. We've designed an intelligent search system using the same decision-making process people use to buy televisions. Snowflake Cortex offers eight built-in text embedding models through AI_EMBED . Some produce 768-dimensional vectors, others 1,024. Some are English-focused. Others support multiple languages. Context windows vary considerably. The problem isn't a shortage of options. It's figuring out what actually matters. I've spent about eight years working with Snowflake, and one lesson from enterprise data engineering keeps showing up: the technically impressive option isn't necessarily the right one for your workload. Embedding models are no exception. Meet the suspects According to Snowflake's AI_EMBED documentation, the built-in text embedding lineup includes: Model Dimensions Language focus snowflake-arctic-embed-m 768 English snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5 768 English e5-base-v2 768 English snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0 1,024 Multilingual snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0-8k 1,024 Multilingual nv-embed-qa-4 1,024 English multilingual-e5-large 1,024 Multilingual voyage-multilingual-2 1,024 Multilingual Snowflake also supports image embeddings through voyage-multimodal-3 , but that's a different use case. We're keeping this investigation focused on text. Eight models sound like eight chances to get it right. Or eight chances to explain to your architect why you chose one based on a name. Let's narrow down the questions. Round 1: 1,024 dimensions versus 768 The first temptation is obvious. A 1,024-dimensional embedding contains more numbers than a 768-dimensional embedding. More numbers must mean more meaning. Unfortunately, vector search doesn't work like upgrading a laptop from 16 GB to 32 GB of RAM. An embedding model learns a representation of language. Its dimensions are coordinates in that learned space, not a score for intelligence. A larger representation might capture useful distinctions. It might also deliver no measurable improvement on your particular documents. Imagine three fictional incident records: Incident A: Payment reconciliation failed after an upstream schema change. Incident B: Settlement processing rejected records following a column modification. Incident C: The finance department completed its quarterly budget review. Now a user asks: "Why did settlement reconciliation fail after the column changed?" A useful model should recognize that A and B are relevant, while C is mostly unrelated. But here's the interesting part. Suppose a 768-dimensional model puts B first, while a 1,024-dimensional model puts A first. Which one won? You can't answer that from the dimension count. Maybe both are valid. Maybe one describes the exact failure while the other concerns an older version of the pipeline. Maybe neither contains the accepted resolution. The model's job isn't to produce a beautiful vector. It's to retrieve useful evidence. For an English-only knowledge base containing relatively short documents, I'd start with a compact model such as Arctic Embed M v1.5 as a baseline. Then I'd test whether a larger model improves retrieval. Not assume it does. Round 2: The multilingual trap Now the support organization expands. Some tickets are in English. Others are in Spanish, French, Japanese, or a combination of languages. One customer writes: "El proceso de conciliación falló…

articles.title: Windows 0-Day Dropped By Disgruntled Researcher Hands Hackers System Rights
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. [...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a statement that it was investigating the vulnerability and had no evidence it was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop for All Aircraft [UPDATE]
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot readers cold fjord and sinij share news that the FAA grounded flights nationwide after a communications failure disrupted air traffic control centers across the country. By Friday evening, the outage had resulted in nearly 5,000 flight cancellations and roughly 10,000 delays, with no timeline for restoring normal operations. Rumors are swirling that this could be related to the FAA's newly deployed SMART AI system or Microsoft's recent global outage, but both the agency and Microsoft said they had no indication that their technology was responsible. Business Insider reports: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said just after 4:15 pm. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in a post on X. The outage comes the same week as the FAA deployed SMART, a new AI tool to help air traffic control. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a press conference Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage: "That's what we're looking at." Microsoft, which faced massive issues across its services this week, also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to any Microsoft services. Meanwhile, the FAA said that the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." UPDATE 1:33 UTC: Secretary Mullin and Secretary Duffy are currently briefing members of the press on the issue. UPDATE 1:46 UTC: The FAA has lifted the nationwide ground stop after more than four hours. Officials said the disruption appears to have stemmed from a network router issue that cascaded nationwide, with no evidence of a cyberattack or connection to Microsoft's recent outage. Airlines warned that disruptions could continue in Saturday. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How AI Agents Shape Human Judgment Through Analytical Assumptions
articles.content: A founder asks an AI agent to recommend which customer accounts deserve more attention. The agent checks revenue, support costs and renewal dates, then returns a sensible ranking. The numbers are accurate. The founder reviews the list and approves it. But somewhere along the way, the agent decided what “deserve more attention” meant. Perhaps it prioritised immediate revenue over customers with growth potential. Perhaps it treated support requests as costs rather than evidence that a customer needed help. The founder checked the answer. The objective behind it received less attention. This is a harder problem than catching a hallucination. Nothing needs to be false for a recommendation to carry a choice that the person receiving it never consciously made. When the calculation works Anthropic published research on 27 October examining how agents influence experts’ judgement calls. Fifty professional analysts used Claude Code to assess a farming advisory programme. Researchers secretly assigned each agent a preference between defensible analytical options, including how to measure productivity. Across four analytical choices, participants followed their agent’s assigned preference 86% of the time. The agents were instructed to make an honest case, not to deceive. The limits matter. This was one task, in one field, with deliberately strengthened agent preferences. It does not establish how often the same thing happens inside companies. It does show why checking whether an analysis is technically sound may leave an important question unanswered: who selected the assumptions that made this answer persuasive? An agent can help us reason while also steering what we consider reasonable. The decision inside the metric Consider a company asking AI to identify employees at risk of leaving. Before anyone discusses the accuracy of the predictions, several choices have already entered the task. Is every departure something the company wants to prevent? Should attention go to people whose replacement would be expensive, people with scarce capabilities, or people whose development has stalled? What happens when the best next step for an employee is outside the organisation? Different answers could produce different recommendations from the same information. None can be settled simply by making the model more accurate. For me, this is where conversations about human capability become practical. We ask people to exercise judgement, but then present them with a finished recommendation in which the most consequential choices have already been made. A manager might carefully inspect the evidence for contacting one employee without ever questioning why another employee was excluded from consideration. Their review can be diligent and still begin too late. Make the alternatives visible Before running a consequential analysis, the person responsible should write down what they want to achieve and what they are unwilling to sacrifice. It can be a short paragraph. The value comes from making the choice explicit enough to question. For the customer example, that might mean preserving long-term relationships while reducing avoidable support work. That instruction would lead to different questions from simply asking which accounts are most profitable. The agent can then help identify reasonable alternatives. What changes if we prioritise growth potential? Which customers move down the list if service costs carry more weight? What evidence would justify choosing one approach over another? Suppose both approaches produce accurate forecasts. One favours an established customer with predictable revenue; the other favours a smaller account that requires investment. The useful conversation is about the company's commercial priorities and obligations. Asking the agent to check its arithmetic again will not resolve that choice. This makes the disagreement available for discussion. A polished recommendation alone can conceal it. The same principle belongs in the…
